chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Al-'Ala' ibn Rawbab from Ibn Muskān from Ibn Abi Ya'fur from Al-Hasan ibn Mahran from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him, 'May God perfect you: A man divorced his wife while she was in a state of purity, without sexual intercourse, with the testimony of two just witnesses.' He said, 'When she enters the third menstruation, her waiting period is completed and she becomes permissible for marriage.' I said to him, 'May God perfect you, indeed the people of Iraq narrate from Ali (peace be upon him) that he said: He has more right to take her back as long as she has not bathed from the third menstruation.' He said, 'They lie.'

key_terms.أَهْلَ الْعِرَاق: People of Iraq (referring to a specific juristic school or view)
key_terms.رَجْعَة: Revocation of divorce (taking back the wife)

ai.seo_question: When does a divorced woman's waiting period end and when does the husband lose the right to take her back if divorced during purity?
ai.summary: This hadith clarifies the precise moment the waiting period (Iddah) concludes for a revocable divorce (Taliq al-Zawj) pronounced during a period of purity without intercourse, establishing that the third menstruation itself marks the end of the period. It highlights a key jurisprudential dispute between the Kufan school, which required the completion of the ritual bath (Ghusl) from the third menses before the husband could remarry, and the Imam's view that the mere onset of the third menstruation suffices. The Imam explicitly rejects the Iraqi tradition attributing the stricter view to Imam Ali, affirming the immediacy of the ruling upon the third menstrual flow.
